enablers: Extended/decentralized collaboration among a breadth of actors (top-down and bottom-up); institutional and organizational diversity (diversity hypothesis); mandatory consultation indicators (GO01, GO02) enabling actor engagement and a "named person" responsible for consultations; knowledge sharing and information exchange; building climate change knowledge and awareness; continuous monitoring and evaluation with reliable access to information; local community inclusion as significant partners; two-way, timely communication; role of BC assessors in distributing/sharing information; making optional indicators (GO03, GO04) mandatory
challenges: Climate change not treated as a serious/priority issue by built environment actors; community consultation not considered a priority (Maguire & Cartwright, 2008); local community lacked knowledge of BC role and consultation processes; poor/ineffective consultation ("a few pictures and a simple explanation... no feedback later on"); lack of continued engagement during occupation; optional (non-mandatory) status of key indicators; developers retaining control and focusing on economic/business aspects; difficulty accessing developers; absence of ongoing monitoring/evaluation post-occupancy; lack of educational/awareness programmes; gap between theory and practice; dependence on experts' personalities
evidenceInPractice: Application of BC at MediaCity, Salford (UK) as exemplar; comparative empirical evidence from Masthusen project, Sweden (Oliver & Pearl, 2018) where BC produced higher engagement but could not guarantee extensive collaboration and community consultation failed; MediaCity flood-protection and water-consumption/recycling facilities perceived as well managed (AG5 positive); experts reported wider inclusion of actors than on conventional projects; but community reported no awareness of consultation, monitoring, or climate learning programmes
indicators: Five AG characteristics (AG1: extended collaboration process; AG2: build knowledge and understanding of CC and adaptation strategies; AG3: shared/participatory ways of knowledge building & awareness; AG4: inclusion of risk monitoring tools for continuous evaluation of development facilities; AG5: focus on developing possible actions in response to environmental change); matrix approach mapping AG characteristics against 4 BC governance indicators (GO01-GO04); three-point rating scale ("+" promotes/no enhancement needed, "o" neutral/further enhancement, "-" hinders/enhancement required) applied to theoretical (manual), expert-questionnaire (percentage/mean thresholds) and community (NVIVO-coded) evaluations
mechanisms: Social learning and iterative learning processes; collaboration/participation and knowledge exchange among diverse actors (formal institutions, informal networks, individuals at multiple scales); decentralized decision-making; institutional/organizational diversity responding to complex systems; continuous monitoring, evaluation and feedback loops; consultation and engagement; information dissemination/communication (two-way)
institutionalEnablers: Mandatory BC governance indicators (Consultation Plan GO01, Consultation and Engagement GO02) requiring a "named person"; presence of required committees (developers, authority, BC actors) promoting knowledge sharing; BC 'International Bespoke' process flexing indicators to local context; multi-actor networks including local authority, developers, environmental agencies; building-scale BREEAM enabling continuous monitoring that could extend to neighbourhood scale; potential council-community-developer partnerships
institutionalConstraints: Optional (non-mandatory) status of Design Review (GO03) and Community Management of Facilities (GO04); BC's optional, non-binding governmental position; developer-dominated governance prioritising economic/business aspects; absence of institutionalised post-occupancy monitoring/evaluation mechanisms; no mandated ongoing community engagement; market-responsive rather than climate-responsive adaptability in review processes; lack of required climate change focus in indicators
powerPolitics: Mentioned; power/politics engaged via top-down vs bottom-up governance dynamics, developers' dominance in decision-making and information control, community exclusion, and BC's "stationary position from the government" and optional status, but not developed as an explicit power-theoretic analytical framework
equity: Mentioned; concern with community inclusion, empowerment, participation, well-being and quality of life (focus group themes); emphasis on including local community as significant/equal partners and two-way communication; notes NSAs' weak focus on social and economic pillars; legitimacy/justice not framed in explicit normative theory (brief citation of Westman 2017 on environmental justice)
relatedConcepts: Resilience (community resilience, resilience management, resilience-based governance); adaptive capacity; sustainability / sustainable development; collaborative/decentralized environmental management; neighbourhood sustainability assessment (NSA); climate change adaptation and mitigation
distinguishedFrom: AG presented as the framework enabling the operationalisation of resilience and adaptive capacity ("setting the concept of resilience into practical terms"); sustainability assessment (NSAs) seen as favouring environmental over social/economic pillars and rarely assessing governance, whereas AG explicitly addresses social adaptation and multi-scale collaborative governance; not a sharply theorised distinction; concepts largely treated as interlinked/complementary rather than differentiated
evidenceType: Mixed; single-case study combining conceptual/theoretical matrix evaluation of tool documentation with qualitative empirical evidence (expert survey/interviews and community focus groups); supplemented by comparative literature (Masthusen, Sweden)
note: Empirical single-case study (MediaCity) integrated with conceptual/theoretical matrix analysis; AG is the dominant analytical frame (Folke et al. 2005 five characteristics). Caveats: small expert sample (13 of 21 target; questionnaire not interviews due to actor unavailability); focus group n=23; text has OCR artifacts (garbled numbers/references, e.g. figures like "8287-8312", "5-7 participants"); percentages in tables are respondent proportions. Normative stance is clearly advocatory toward enhancing BC to enable AG.

title: Water, resilience and the law: From general concepts and governance design principles to actionable mechanisms
geographicLabel: Multiple jurisdictions used as best-practice examples; western USA; Spain; South Africa; Tanzania (Pangani River Basin); European Union (Water Framework Directive); Scotland; Chile; Australia (Victoria, NWI); Finland; also references to transboundary basins (Danube, Indus); Bangladesh
sector: Water governance and management; water law/policy; climate change adaptation in the water resources sector
method: Conceptual/qualitative review combined with illustrative comparative legal analysis; review and synthesis of adaptive/integrative water governance and resilience-adaptive-capacity literature to derive guiding principles (Table A1); identification and evaluation of "best practice examples" of legal mechanisms across jurisdictions; assessment of mechanisms against categories of climate uncertainty (Tables 1 and 2); underpinned by ACQWA project governance research including interviews
unitOfAnalysis: Legal mechanisms/instruments (policy, legislation, regulation, property/use rights) within water governance frameworks across different jurisdictions; assessed against adaptive governance guiding principles
level: Multilevel (explicitly spanning local/basin, national, regional/EU, and international/transboundary scales; subsidiarity emphasised)
framework: Social-ecological resilience theory; adaptive capacity, adaptive management, adaptive governance and adaptive/integrated water resources management (IWRM) literature; law as a complex adaptive system; panarchy; four derived guiding principles (iterativity, flexibility, connectivity, subsidiarity)
enablers: Flexibility in social systems and institutions; openness of institutions/extensive participation; effective multi-level governance (connectivity and subsidiarity); iterative learning and adaptability; time-bound review periods with potential reallocation; varied/variable use rights and permit systems; risk apportionment across actors; matching institutions to appropriate scales; stable/predictable higher-level structures enabling lower-level experimentation; monitoring and data sharing; financial and technical capacity; public availability/exchange of data (Aarhus Convention, WISE)
challenges: Tension between legal predictability/stability and ecological complexity/flexibility; generalised principles lacking clarity/detail for operationalisation; gaps between legislation and institutional capacity to implement/enforce; irreversible changes/regime shifts beyond past coping ranges (greater warming); optional rather than mandatory secondary legislation (Tanzania) undermining critical concepts; coexistence of unaccountable private water rights (Spain, Chile); difficulty of horizontal inter-sectoral and transboundary coordination; data limitations (incomplete, incompatible formats); weak legal foundation for WUAs; water rights trading less useful as uncertainty increases; sovereignty/ownership of hydrological data; non-stationarity undermining projections based on historical data
evidenceInPractice: Concrete legal mechanisms: South African NWA fixed-term licences reviewed every 5 years and variable (ss.28,31,49); EU WFD programmes of measures revised every 6 years; Tanzanian water resources management plans reviewed every 3-5 years (WRMA 2009); Scotland primary/secondary legislation split (WEWS 2003); Chile 1981 Water Code amended 2005; Australian NWI risk apportionment and Victoria's share-based entitlements with 50-year planning and water trading; Finland variable rights without time limit; Australia Bureau of Meteorology General Purpose Water Accounting; EU WISE; Danube Convention data exchange; western USA prior appropriation; Pangani River Basin WUA (Tanzania)
indicators: Operationalised via four guiding principles (iterativity, flexibility, connectivity, subsidiarity) each defined and mapped to "actionable governance mechanisms" in Table 1; further assessed in Table 2 against three categories of uncertainty (stationarity with predictable uncertainty; broader range of uncertainty with reduced predictability; irreversibility/regime shifts); initial synthesis of indicators/principles in Table A1 (supplementary materials)
mechanisms: Iterative review and revision processes (feedback loops incorporating new science/data); social/iterative learning and adaptability; multi-level (polycentric) governance via subsidiarity and connectivity; risk diversification/apportionment; flexible/variable rights and permit systems; monitoring and data exchange enabling adaptation; balancing stability with flexibility ("stability within change")
institutionalEnablers: Blend of stable/predictable higher-level structures (primary legislation, government institutions) with flexible lower-level provisions (secondary legislation, regional/local regulations); administrative and property-rights frameworks that allow variation of use rights; permit/authorisation systems treated as revocable property rights; framework legislation (WFD) enabling local implementation; national databases/monitoring networks; transboundary agreements with data-exchange requirements
institutionalConstraints: Codified/consolidated legal systems with little scope for modification (South Africa, Chile); optional (non-mandatory) secondary legislation left unenacted (Tanzania classification of waters); coexisting unaccountable private water rights (Spain, Chile); torpid development of secondary legislation in less developed jurisdictions; weak policy frameworks lacking deadlines/reporting (Bangladesh Coastal Zone Policy 2005); insufficient institutional capacity, financing and legal foundations (WUAs); incompatible/incomplete data infrastructure; perpetual/immutable or absolute rights; sovereignty constraints on data
powerPolitics: Mentioned - power and politics appear as "political realities" limiting basin-scale coordination and states not ceding responsibility to supra-national institutions; note that "Power should also be delegated as part of this management transfer process" for WUAs; a "shift of burden to higher levels of governance" for global feedbacks; but power is not the central analytical concern
equity: Equity, legitimacy and justice are addressed: South African variations restricted "in the interests of equity"; use entitlements as share ensuring scarcity is "more equitably apportioned"; reserve for basic human needs and aquatic ecosystems; Aarhus Convention on access to information/participation/justice; public confidence in states' management; Cosens' work on legitimacy cited; equity contrasted with Tanzania where equity-protecting mechanisms are absent
relatedConcepts: Resilience (social-ecological); adaptive capacity; adaptive management; adaptive and integrated water resources management (IWRM); law as a complex adaptive system; participatory/collaborative water management (Water User Associations); property rights theory
distinguishedFrom: Adaptive governance is presented as one of a family of "adaptive" approaches, distinguished from adaptive management (each management step an opportunity for further adaptive learning) and characterised specifically as collaboration/cooperation across levels and agencies with overlapping authority (p.99); the paper distinguishes resilience of the governing system (laws, policy, institutions) from resilience of the governed system (rivers, groundwater, ecosystems) citing Armitage (p.100); it positions its focus on features of law enabling adaptive governance rather than on resilience of law itself; otherwise the concepts are treated as closely interlinked rather than sharply differentiated
evidenceType: Mixed - primarily theoretical/conceptual (literature review deriving principles) underpinned by illustrative comparative empirical legal examples ("best practice examples") across jurisdictions; not systematic empirical measurement
note: Article's dominant twin frame is resilience-and-the-law plus adaptive governance principles; AG is central (not a passing mention) as it supplies the analytical guiding principles used to evaluate legal mechanisms; largely conceptual/applied with comparative illustrative legal examples rather than primary empirical case study; no single study site; page numbers cited are the journal's printed pages 98-110; some OCR artefacts in original (e.g., missing hyphens/en-dashes)
